label: Title
notes: Open the lecture as a change of language: the chapter turns motion, maps, equations, and differential operators into the single object called a tangent vector. The five-part map lets students see that derivations are not an isolated definition; they feed rank tests, bundles, partitions of unity, flows, and brackets.

label: Derivations
notes: Start with the algebraic definition because it is the coordinate-free anchor for the chapter. A tangent vector at p is not drawn as a little arrow first; it is a rule that differentiates germs and obeys the Leibniz identity. The arrow picture will reappear after this definition has earned its invariance.

label: Differential
notes: The pushforward is defined by asking the old derivation to act on a pulled-back target function. This is the key teaching move: the formula is not a matrix formula yet, it is a way to transport first-order tests through a smooth map. Coordinates later reveal the same operation as the Jacobian.

label: Chain Rule
notes: Use the commutative diagram to make the chain rule look inevitable. Pull functions back through G and then F, or push a tangent vector forward through F and then G; both descriptions encode the same first-order information. This is the first glimpse of tangent spaces behaving functorially.

label: Coordinate Bases
notes: Once coordinates are chosen, derivations acquire a basis and look like column vectors of partial derivatives. The transition rule is the important invariant content: a different chart changes the coefficients by the Jacobian of the coordinate change, so the tangent vector itself is not tied to one coordinate grid.

label: Curves
notes: Curves connect the algebraic and geometric pictures. The velocity c prime at t is the pushforward of d over dt, and applying a map to the curve gives the same answer as applying the differential to the velocity. The check values show the two computations agree exactly in the notebook model.

label: Rank
notes: Rank is the chapter's local diagnostic. For the square map shown here, the determinant of the Jacobian is positive away from the origin and zero at the origin, so the differential sees exactly where the map stops being locally full rank. This visual prepares the regular and critical level-set contrast.

label: Regular Level Sets
notes: Regular level sets turn equations into manifolds because the differential has enough independent rows to solve for the missing coordinates. The tangent space is the kernel of the differential. On the critical crossing, the kernel test loses its expected dimension, and the picture stops being a clean embedded curve at the origin.

label: Constant Rank
notes: The constant-rank theorem is the stabilizing result behind many examples. If the rank is locally fixed, charts on source and target straighten the map into projection onto the first k coordinates followed by zeros. Use this to name the regular-submanifold model: locally a subset is a coordinate slice, with the last coordinates set to zero. Regular level sets and embedding images earn their manifold structure by reducing to that model.

label: Immersions And Embeddings
notes: Separate three issues that students often blend together: injectivity of the differential, surjectivity of the differential, and global topological behavior. An immersion can pass the tangent-space test and still self-intersect. An embedding adds the topological condition needed for the image to inherit the correct manifold structure.

label: Tangent Plane
notes: The surface example returns to the arrow intuition after the invariant machinery is in place. A tangent plane is spanned by coordinate velocity vectors, and for a level surface it is also a kernel. The point is that both the parametrized and implicit descriptions agree through the same differential language.

label: Tangent Bundle
notes: Move from one tangent space to all tangent spaces at once. The tangent bundle is a disjoint union, or equivalently the set of pairs consisting of a base point and a tangent vector at that point. The projection remembers the base point, while local coordinates turn the bundle into U times R to the n. This is the local triviality pattern that will guide vector bundles and sections.

label: Sections And Frames
notes: A vector field is a smooth choice of tangent vector at every point, so it is a section of the tangent bundle. In a coordinate chart, a field is a sum of coefficient functions times coordinate basis fields. Frames package local bases of sections and make computations look like moving linear algebra.

label: Partitions Of Unity
notes: Partitions of unity are the chapter's glue. The conditions of nonnegativity, local finiteness, unit sum, and support control let local constructions be blended without losing smoothness. This is why bump functions appear next to tangent bundles: they make local frames and local data usable on the whole manifold.

label: Flows
notes: Vector fields are not only derivations; they generate motion. Integral curves solve an ordinary differential equation on the manifold, and the local flow records all such solutions at once. The identity and composition laws hold where both sides are defined, which is why local flows behave like partial one-parameter groups.

label: Lie Bracket And Related Fields
notes: The Lie bracket measures the first-order defect in commuting two vector-field directions. It is defined as a commutator of differential operators and can also be detected by a small flow commutator. Pause on the pushforward warning: if F sends two source points p and q to the same target point, then F star of X at p and at q must agree before they define one target vector field. Diffeomorphisms avoid the ambiguity, and F-relatedness is the replacement condition for general smooth maps.

label: Summary And Inspection Targets
notes: Close by asking students to inspect the same object from multiple angles: a tangent vector can be a derivation, a curve velocity, a coordinate vector, or an element of a fiber. The local artifacts give concrete checks for rank, curve pushforward, level regularity, partition sums, and Lie bracket computation.
